title: Explain why `peek()` should NOT be used for side effects in production code (may be skipped by the pipeline).
shortTitle: Explain why peek() should NOT be used for side effects in production code

s1_definition.profdef: `peek` is an intermediate operation whose execution is not guaranteed for every element. Since Java 9, when the stream is SIZED and the terminal operation does not need element values (for example `count()`), the pipeline may skip `peek` entirely. Relying on `peek` for business side-effects therefore produces unreliable behaviour.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya watches account forms on a belt and jots notes. But if the bank only wants a head count, the belt operator may just read the counter and never let the forms pass her desk at all — so her notes would be empty. You cannot trust note-taking to actually record every form; use a proper desk whose job is recording.
s1_definition.oneliner: The pipeline may legally skip `peek`, so never put real work in it — use `map`, `forEach`, or a collector instead.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `peek` is an intermediate operation whose execution is not guaranteed for every element. Since Java 9, when the stream is SIZED and the terminal operation does not need element values (for example `count()`), the pipeline may skip `peek` entirely. Relying on `peek` for business side-effects therefore produces unreliable behaviour.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Priya watches account forms on a belt and jots notes. But if the bank only wants a head count, the belt operator may just read the counter and never let the forms pass her desk at all — so her notes would be empty. You cannot trust note-taking to actually record every form; use a proper desk whose job is recording.

**One line to remember:** The pipeline may legally skip `peek`, so never put real work in it — use `map`, `forEach`, or a collector instead.

sections.s2_technical:
The Stream contract says `peek` exists mainly to support debugging. The Java 9 release note made this concrete: for a SIZED stream, `count()` can return the size without traversing elements, so any `peek` upstream is never invoked. For example `List.of("a","b").stream().peek(System.out::println).count()` prints nothing on Java 9 and later, because the size is known to be two without walking the elements.

This means if you write real side-effects in peek — saving to a database, incrementing a counter, sending a notification — those effects may silently not happen depending on the terminal operation and JDK version. The correct place for a transforming side-effect is `map`, and for a terminal side-effect it is `forEach` or a custom collector, both of which are guaranteed to run for every element.

The senior nuance is that this is not a bug but a documented optimization, and it makes peek unsafe for anything the program depends on. A reviewer should flag any peek that mutates state or performs I/O as a correctness risk, not just a style issue.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A developer at the National Bank of India put an audit-log write inside peek, and after a Java upgrade some audit entries went missing because the terminal count skipped peek.

This is exactly why peek must not carry side-effects — the fix is to move the audit write into a guaranteed stage like map or forEach so every element is processed.

The code shows the buggy count-skips-peek behaviour and the corrected forEach version.
sections.s5_journey:
Input: three transactions TXN1, TXN2, TXN3.

Step 1: The buggy pipeline streams the list and calls peek to increment an audit counter, then ends with count().

Step 2: Because the list is SIZED, count() returns three without walking the elements, so peek never runs and the audit counter stays at zero.

Step 3: The fixed version uses forEach, which the contract guarantees to run for every element, so the counter correctly becomes three.

```
WARNING: count=3 but audited via peek=0 (may be 0 — peek skipped!)
INFO: audited via forEach=3 (always correct)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  [TXN1,TXN2,TXN3]
    │ peek(increment)   ← may be SKIPPED when terminal is count()
    │ count() → 3 (size known, no traversal)
    ▼
  audited counter = 0   ← effects lost

  FIX:
  [TXN1,TXN2,TXN3] → forEach(increment) → counter = 3  ✓ guaranteed
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```
  ═══ HLD — Audit Write Placement ═══

  BAD:  stream → peek(audit) → count   → audit may never run
  GOOD: stream → forEach(audit)        → audit always runs
     side-effects belong in guaranteed stages, not peek
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — why peek is unsafe for side-effects ═══

  ┌─ Stream contract ──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ peek is "mainly to support debugging"                       │
  │ Java 9+: SIZED stream + count() → elements not traversed    │
  │   → upstream peek is NOT invoked                            │
  │ side-effects in peek: save/notify/counter → may be lost     │
  │ correct stages: map (transform), forEach (terminal effect)  │
  │ documented optimization, not a bug → treat as correctness   │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Call chain (buggy):
  1. stream().peek(increment)
  2. count() → returns size, skips peek
  3. counter unchanged → audit lost
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Peek is documented as an intermediate operation that exists mainly to support debugging, and crucially the pipeline is allowed to skip it. Since Java 9, if the stream is sized and the terminal operation is count, the runtime can return the size without ever traversing the elements, which means any peek upstream is never invoked. So if I place a real side-effect in peek — writing an audit record, incrementing a counter, sending a notification — that effect can silently fail to happen depending on the terminal operation and the JDK version.

I learned this the hard way on a banking project where an audit write sat inside peek and, after a Java upgrade, audit entries went missing because a count-based terminal skipped the peek stage entirely. The fix was to move the side-effect into a guaranteed stage: map for a transformation that also records, or forEach and custom collectors for terminal effects, all of which are contractually run for every element.

The senior point I stress is that this is not a bug but a documented optimization, which is exactly why it is dangerous — the code looks correct and often works, until a terminal operation or JDK version changes the traversal. So in review I flag any peek that mutates state or performs input-output as a correctness risk and insist side-effects live only in stages the contract promises to execute.
